title: Vote commitment formats diverge across exported paths

sourceLocations.note: Upgraded session-bound commitment encoding and shared domain.
Commit admission performs only hash-shape validation, then reveal admission recomputes the upgraded format.
No admitted reveal makes tally finalization fail.
Exported legacy producer reuses the same domain with an outcome/salt-only text encoding.
Legacy producer is part of the public package API.

triageResult.reasoning: The package exports `hashCommit` (dispute.ts) and `hashCourtVoteCommit` (courtVoteMachine.ts) under the same `BAO-Court/VoteCommit/v1` domain, but they encode different preimages: `hashCommit` only writes `outcome` and `salt` as text, while `hashCourtVoteCommit` writes `sessionHash` as hex, `outcome` as text, and `salt` as hex. The vote machine's `accept_commit` only checks the 64-character hex shape (courtVoteMachine.ts:302-304), so a legacy-format commit is accepted. `accept_reveal` then recomputes the session-bound format and rejects the reveal (courtVoteMachine.ts:357-365), and `finalize_tally` fails with zero valid reveals (courtVoteMachine.ts:400-406). The legacy helper is part of the public API (index.ts:169-177) and used in the simulator and coordinator (scripts/simulateCourt.ts:160, appealCoordinator.ts:479), so mixed deployments are realistically reachable. The documented fix intent (docs/FIXES-2026-08-18.md:159-160) confirms the two paths were meant to share the same domain, making this a real protocol incompatibility.

description: The repository exposes two vote-commit producers that use the same `BAO-Court/VoteCommit/v1` domain but encode different preimages. `hashCourtVoteCommit` includes a length-prefixed binary `sessionHash`, UTF-8 `outcome`, and binary `salt`, whereas the exported legacy `hashCommit` includes only length-prefixed text `outcome` and text `salt`. A legacy commit is still accepted by the machine's syntactic 64-character hash check, but when the corresponding reveal reaches `reduceCourtVoteMachine`, the machine recomputes the session-bound digest and rejects it as mismatched. The divergence is therefore an end-to-end producer/verifier incompatibility rather than merely an undocumented direct-helper validation difference.
impact: A host that uses the exported `hashCommit` or an integration built around the legacy imperative API to publish commitments cannot complete an upgraded `courtVoteMachine` ceremony: valid reveals are rejected and `finalize_tally` eventually fails because no valid reveal was admitted. Mixed deployments can also produce inconsistent tallies, with upgraded nodes excluding commitments that legacy nodes consider valid; any downstream resolution waiting on the upgraded tally is delayed or unavailable.
rootCause: The legacy and upgraded commitment APIs share `BAO-Court/VoteCommit/v1` but disagree on both field set and field encoding. The machine has no protocol-version discriminator that could reject legacy commitments before ceremony processing or route them to a matching verifier.

fix.explanation: Separated the sessionless legacy commitment into its own domain and added an explicit digest-format discriminator: machine commitments set the discriminator bit, legacy commitments clear it, and the vote reducer rejects legacy commitments at admission instead of storing commitments that can never reveal.

title: Post-Deadline Close Is Intentional Catch-Up

sourceLocations.note: Ticks preserve `reveal_closed` but expire unfinished phases at or after the deadline.
Closure is legal at or after the reveal deadline only from `reveal_open`.
Finalization is legal only from the closed phase and rejects an empty ledger.

triageResult.reasoning: The regression documentation explicitly states that close_reveals is legal at or after the deadline and that tick must preserve reveal_closed for finalization. The reducer implements exactly this behavior while accept_reveal independently rejects deadline-or-later reveals.

description: The post-deadline `close_reveals` transition itself is a deliberate catch-up operation, not a deadline bypass. It requires the machine already to be in `reveal_open`, rejects only times before `revealDeadline`, and changes the phase to `reveal_closed` without adding any reveal. `accept_reveal` independently rejects timestamps at or after the deadline, and `tick` explicitly leaves `reveal_closed` untouched so finalization remains possible. Therefore a coordinator that has not dispatched `tick` may legitimately close at the deadline or later and then finalize previously accepted reveals. If `tick` has already moved the unfinished machine to `expired`, terminal-phase rejection correctly prevents a later close.
impact: This boundary preserves valid pre-deadline reveals when the close event is delayed and does not itself admit new late reveals. The security problem is instead the separately reported non-monotonic timestamp and late-open behavior, not closing after the deadline without a prior tick.
rootCause: No defect is present in the late-close boundary; it intentionally separates deadline closure from timeout processing so a close received after the deadline can finalize a frozen ledger.

title: Unverified Support Evidence Can Certify False Tallies

sourceLocations.note: Reveal admission validates IDs per participant and detects conflicts only by participant index.
Winning reveal IDs are collected without global uniqueness checks, then the machine's verdict is finalized.
The exported dispute commitment hashes the caller-supplied support list without evidence or uniqueness validation.
The signing message is built from the caller-provided verdict hash and signed without recomputing the underlying tally.
Kind-39007 validation checks verdict-hash format, tag/content agreement, message binding, and signature, but not the hash against supporting reveals.
Settlement checks signed message fields and the group signature but does not recompute hashDisputeVerdict.
The supplied supporting IDs are published as mention tags and content without validation.

triageResult.reasoning:
Draft claim: `valid` — `hashDisputeVerdict` and downstream consumers accept fabricated/duplicate supporting event IDs without evidence or uniqueness checks, allowing false tallies to be certified. Verdict attacked: `valid` / `other-category`. Scope read: terminal actor is the caller that supplies `supportingEventIds` and `verdictHash` to `hashDisputeVerdict` (courtVoteMachine.ts:166) and the signing path (signing.ts:192-257), and the publisher that builds the kind-39007 event (events.ts:763-780). Sinks are `validateAttestationEvent` (validator.ts:92-161) and `FrostAppealCoordinator.settleAppeal` (appealCoordinator.ts:727-773). Refutation on materiality: the cited downstream consumers do not consume the supporting IDs in any value-moving, authorization, or liveness branch. `settleAppeal` (appealCoordinator.ts:727-773) only validates `attestation.marketId`, `attestation.message`, `attestation.verdictHash`, `attestation.signature`, `attestation.groupPubkey`, and `attestation.outcome`; it never reads `attestation.supportingEventIds`. `FrostAppealWatcher.handleEvent` (appealWatcher.ts:191-215) returns `outcome`, `marketId`, `disputeEventId`, `groupPubkey`, and `eventId` but no supporting IDs. `validateAttestationEvent` (validator.ts:92-161) checks the `verdict` tag format and that the FROST message binds it, but does not inspect the `e` mention tags. `buildDisputeAttestationEvent` (events.ts:763-780) only writes the IDs to tags and content. Since the only material branch is the threshold-signed outcome, fabricated or duplicated IDs can only corrupt an evidentiary field; they cannot alter the settlement/resolution outcome or authorize an unauthorized transfer. The entire surviving impact is therefore an evidentiary mismatch, sub-material for a security finding.
Evidence: appealCoordinator.ts:727-773; appealWatcher.ts:191-215; events.ts:763-780; validator.ts:92-161; signing.ts:192-257; courtVoteMachine.ts:166,429-433

description: `hashDisputeVerdict` treats every supporting ID as an opaque caller-supplied value: it copies and sorts the list, encodes its length, and hashes it without enforcing unique canonical event IDs or checking that the IDs identify authenticated reveal events. The vote reducer validates an event ID only within each reveal and prevents conflicting repeats by participant index, but it does not prevent two different participant indices from contributing the same event ID to the final support list. The downstream dispute signing path accepts a caller-provided `verdictHash` and signs it, while `validateAttestationEvent` and `FrostAppealCoordinator.settleAppeal` verify only the signed hash/message and do not recompute it from the supporting reveal ledger. `buildDisputeAttestationEvent` then publishes the unverified IDs as evidence tags and content. Consequently, a party supplying the signing inputs can obtain a valid kind-39007 attestation whose commitment counts fabricated or duplicated evidence rather than the actual winning tally.
impact: Threshold signers can certify a false tally commitment while the signature remains valid, and consumers can accept it as a court resolution because the signature and hash shape pass their checks. A downstream settlement or appeal handler that relies on the attested outcome can therefore act on an outcome or support count not established by the public vote ledger.
rootCause: The commitment API and its consumers authenticate the hash value, not the evidence and set semantics that the hash is intended to represent. Duplicate detection is scoped to participant indices, and no downstream boundary validates or recomputes the supporting event-ID set before signing or settlement.

title: Empty Dispute Filter Broadens Results

sourceLocations.note: `disputeId` is optional but its filtering branch is truthiness-gated, allowing an empty supplied value to skip the filter.

triageResult.reasoning: Dispute filter at courtSigner.ts:252 uses truthiness check `if (options?.disputeId)` instead of presence check. An explicitly supplied empty string `disputeId: ''` skips the filter and returns verified rumors across all disputes, including those without a dispute tag. This violates the advertised batch filter contract and can leak private rumors across dispute boundaries when a host passes an empty or untrusted identifier.

description: An explicitly supplied empty `options.disputeId` disables dispute filtering because the implementation uses a truthiness test instead of testing whether the option was supplied. Under the documented batch contract, an absent dispute filter accepts all rumors, while a supplied filter must require the first `dispute` tag to equal the supplied value. Passing `{ disputeId: '' }` takes the absent-filter branch and returns every verified rumor, including other disputes and rumors without a dispute tag. This is a filter-bypass difference between a supplied empty identifier and an omitted option.
impact: If a host accepts a dispute identifier from a request or another untrusted source, an empty value can broaden the returned result set across dispute boundaries. Downstream code may process or disclose private rumors that it intended to scope to one dispute.
rootCause: The dispute filter conflates an absent option with a supplied falsy string through a truthiness check.

fix.explanation: Treat disputeId as an active filter whenever it is supplied, including the empty string, while preserving omitted-option behavior.

title: Regex Validation Coerces Non-String Keys

sourceLocations.note: `HEX_64.test` is used without a `typeof value === 'string'` check.
Validated peer value is forwarded to the signer without runtime normalization.

triageResult.reasoning: assertHex64 uses regex test without explicit typeof string check, but the regex still validates the exact string content. No demonstrated path to cryptographic bypass, inconsistent peer selection, or cross-principal impact; downstream signer either coerces to the same validated string or throws. Type-safety gap with no reachable security impact in this component.

description: `assertHex64` is typed as receiving a string, but its runtime implementation calls `RegExp.prototype.test` directly without first checking `typeof value === 'string'`. JavaScript coerces non-string values supplied at runtime before testing them, so an object with a custom `toString()` returning 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters can pass this check. The original object is then forwarded unchanged to `CourtEventSigner.nip44Encrypt` or `nip44Decrypt`, despite the interface requiring a string. This defeats the intended exact-runtime-type boundary and leaves behavior dependent on the downstream signer’s coercion or serialization.
impact: A caller able to invoke the JavaScript API with non-string values can pass a value that is not the validated canonical key type into an external signer. This can cause type confusion, inconsistent peer selection, or downstream exceptions; no direct cryptographic authorization bypass is established by the local code.
rootCause: The canonical regex check omits an explicit runtime string-type guard and does not forward a normalized string after validation.

rootCause: A non-cryptographic PRNG is used for a value explicitly intended to provide timestamp privacy randomization.

impact: An attacker able to control the batch options can terminate processing of a batch that contains at least one valid rumor, causing a denial of service for the associated inbox or protocol worker. The exception also bypasses the intended per-wrap graceful-rejection behavior and may become an unhandled promise rejection at the host boundary.
rootCause: The batch API relies on an erased array type for `options.kinds` and performs an unchecked method call at the filtering boundary. Filter validation is absent and no batch-level catch isolates malformed options.

fix.explanation: Runtime-check the signer-backed batch kind filter with Array.isArray before using Array.prototype.includes, treating malformed non-array values as an absent filter so they cannot abort processing of valid wraps.

The reducer's publish handler does check only phase==='aggregate', truthy signature, and syntactically valid attestationEventId (courtSigningMachine.ts:374-382), and it accepts any caller-supplied state object without re-validating lifecycle invariants. However, a whole-repo search shows CourtSigningMachineState and its attestation_published/attestationEventId fields are only consumed in tests and poc files (courtSigningMachine.ts itself, __tests__/courtSigningMachine.test.ts, __tests__/poc.test.ts, poc*.ts, and index.ts re-exports). Consequently the surviving impact is a state-integrity violation in a pure reducer API with no material in-repo consumer, and the described attack path remains below the materiality bar.

description: `reduceCourtSigningMachine` accepts a caller-supplied state object but validates neither its integrity nor the phase-specific invariants that creation and prior reducer transitions normally establish. A rehydrated object can claim `phase: 'aggregate'`, contain any truthy 64-byte-looking `signature`, and retain a chosen valid deadline without containing threshold-many commitments or partials. The documented architecture explicitly has hosts persist returned states, making persistence restoration an input boundary rather than an unreachable internal representation.
impact: A host that restores attacker-modified or corrupted reducer snapshots can be driven into a published-attestation state without satisfying the signing lifecycle or producing a valid FROST signature. rootCause: State-machine invariants are enforced only along the normal in-memory transition path. `reduceCourtSigningMachine` trusts persisted runtime state and does not validate its immutable configuration, phase/data consistency, threshold evidence, or aggregate signature before using it as authority.

title: Settlement proceeds after failed attestation publication

sourceLocations.note: Signs the event, detects that no relay acknowledged it, but returns the signed event after only logging a warning.
Unconditionally marks the appeal attestation as published after awaiting the publication helper.
The next lifecycle step releases backup stakes and settles the appeal based only on the local published phase.

triageResult.reasoning: design-decision rejection lacks a threat model for the intent/scope claim. Original reasoning: The behavior matches the documented, intentionally demo/integration-test design of the coordinator. appealCoordinator.ts:15-22 states it is a single-process coordinator intended for demos and integration tests, and that with no relayPool/empty relayUrls the full ceremony runs in-process with events signed but not broadcast. The publication helper at appealCoordinator.ts:263-268 detects all-rejected publishes and only warns. The local phase transition then advances to 'attestation_published' and 'settled', but the actual downstream settlement authority, settleAppeal() at appealCoordinator.ts:710-779, independently validates the attestation signature, verdict hash, message binding, and group key before releasing backup stakes or settling. The coordinator holds no user funds (README.md:7-9), and releaseBackupStakes() only emits a notification. Therefore the surviving effect is a local state/event-emit change with no in-scope cross-system authorization or value transfer gated on it.

description: The coordinator treats an attempted relay publication as successful even when every configured relay rejects the event. `publishEvent()` signs the attestation, waits for `Promise.allSettled`, computes that no relay acknowledged it, and only logs a warning before returning the signed event. The signing phase then unconditionally changes the appeal to `attestation_published`, and the next tick advances that appeal to `settled`; no event lookup or successful-publication gate intervenes. This is distinct from the documented empty/no-transport demo mode: it also occurs with a configured relay pool and a total relay failure, where the attestation is not externally available.

Relays, watchers, and downstream settlement services cannot recover the supposedly published event from the reported lifecycle transition, creating a liveness and cross-system state divergence that can strand or incorrectly advance an appeal.
rootCause: `publishEvent()` does not fail or return a publication-success result when all relay acknowledgements fail, while the caller equates a returned signed event with successful publication. The lifecycle transition lacks an independent event-existence or publication-success check.

title: Publication notification reports event kind as ID

sourceLocations.note: The signed Nostr event is returned from the publication helper, including its actual ID.
The returned event is discarded and `attestationEvent.kind` is emitted as `attestationEventId`.

triageResult.reasoning: The finding is correct that the code at appealCoordinator.ts:560-570 discards the signed NostrEvent returned by publishEvent() and emits attestationEventId: attestationEvent.kind (the constant 39007) instead of the signed event's content-addressed id. The courtSigningMachine reducer validates a host-supplied attestationEventId against a hex-32 syntax check, but it is not fed by the coordinator emission. The mismatch is therefore an observability/notification quality issue, not a material security vulnerability in scoped logic.

The scoped reducer does not create this mismatch; its host-supplied ID is intentionally a pure, syntactically checked reference, but this local publication consumer supplies a value that is not an event identifier.
impact: A host that persists the coordinator event or uses `data.attestationEventId` for relay lookup, deduplication, audit linkage, or attestation retrieval receives a non-ID constant shared by all kind-39007 attestations. title: Unverified Partials Can Publish Forged Attestations

sourceLocations.note: `accept_partial` checks only syntax and frozen-index membership before storing the partial.
`aggregate` and `publish` perform no FROST or publication verification.
The separate signing consumer performs the missing partial and final-signature checks, but the reducer does not call it.

triageResult.reasoning:
The finding correctly observes that reduceCourtSigningMachine stores partial signatures and accepts aggregate/publish events after only syntactic and phase checks, but it mischaracterizes this as a security defect in the scoped reducer. The module header explicitly states the reducer is a pure state machine that performs no FROST cryptographic verification and that the boundary must verify partials before dispatching (courtSigningMachine.ts:16-18). The code shows the opposite invariant: the hash is an attempt identifier created from the configured participant roster (the README's 'signerSet'), while the runtime subset is captured separately in finalizedSignerSet and enforced when admitting partials. The actual FROST commitment context is bound by the collected commitment set in the FROST layer, not by this application-level hash. No reducer or protocol-parser code reads signingSessionHash for any security or liveness decision, so the described 'mixing' cannot happen inside the library and cannot produce an invalid signature; the only surviving effect is a naming/documentation ambiguity.
Evidence: courtSigningMachine.ts:127-148 (hashCourtSigningSession comment calls it the binding of every field that defines one signing attempt and encodes the configured participantIndices roster, not finalizedSignerSet); courtSigningMachine.ts:311-334 (close_commitments derives finalizedSignerSet from collected commitments and accept_partial gates on that set); signing.ts:259-291 (aggregateAttestation builds the FROST group signing context from the actual commitment set and verifies each partial against that context); validator.ts:164-167 (final Schnorr signature is verified against the attestation message); grep for signingSessionHash shows only the state declaration at courtSigningMachine.ts:62, creation at courtSigningMachine.ts:218, and tests — no internal security/liveness consumer.

description: The signing-session identifier is computed from the full configured `participantIndices` roster, while commitment closure permits any threshold-sized subset and stores that subset separately as `finalizedSignerSet`. Consequently, two coordinators can create machines with the same `signingSessionHash` and same attempt parameters but finalize different signer sets, such as `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` for a three-member roster with threshold two. The strict event binding also binds only session, suite, attempt, dispute, juror, and keys; it does not carry the finalized signer set or the computed signing-session hash. The resulting transcript identifier does not uniquely identify the FROST commitment context that later partial signatures and aggregation are supposed to use.
impact: Hosts or relays that use `signingSessionHash` as the attempt/replay identity can conflate distinct commitment contexts and mix events from competing threshold subsets. The mixed context cannot produce a coherent FROST signature and can cause attestation liveness failure or inconsistent audit/recovery decisions; the issue is especially relevant when multiple coordinators independently close the same attempt.
rootCause: The hash input and the state transition use different definitions of the signing signer set. The actual frozen commitment owner set is not bound into the session identity or the strict protocol-event binding.

sourceLocations.note: The reducer accepts caller-supplied state without runtime shape validation.

description: `reduceCourtSigningMachine` treats the supplied state as a trusted in-memory object and performs no runtime validation of the persisted commitment array before using it. impact: A malformed persisted signing state can crash the host while processing a live commitment, or make the attempt appear threshold-ready while it can never collect enough distinct partial signatures. title: Coercion Bypasses Canonical Hash Validation

sourceLocations.note: Session hash regex validation stores the untyped original value.
Transcript and candidate-key validation has the same coercion behavior.
Certification uses strict equality against the potentially non-string stored transcript.

triageResult.reasoning: The reducer validates `sessionHash`, `transcriptHash`, and `candidateGroupPubkey` using `RegExp.prototype.test` without first enforcing primitive `string` type. `RegExp.prototype.test` coerces operands via `ToString`, so boxed `String` objects or single-element arrays containing valid lowercase hex pass the regex. The original non-primitive value is then stored in state. Later, `accept_certification` compares the incoming primitive certification hash with the stored value using strict equality, which returns `true` (i.e., "different") across primitive/boxed types even when the textual content is identical. This causes an otherwise unanimous ceremony to transition to `aborted_peer` and blame the certifier. A live reproduction confirmed this exact path: a boxed `String` transcript in `finalize_transcript` followed by a primitive string in `accept_certification` produced `phase: 'aborted_peer'` with blame on the certifier. The host is explicitly not trusted to bypass coded validation, making this a real reducer-level defect.

description: Canonical hash and key checks use `RegExp.test` without first requiring primitive strings. JavaScript coerces boxed strings, one-element arrays, and other coercible inputs for regex matching, but the reducer stores the original value. A boxed or array transcript that represents valid lowercase hex can therefore pass finalization, while a later primitive-string certification of the same bytes fails strict equality and aborts the ceremony. The same issue can persist non-string session hashes or candidate keys into state typed as canonical strings.
impact: An attacker controlling deserialized events or configuration can induce false transcript conflicts and force an otherwise valid ceremony to abort. It can also propagate noncanonical key/hash values into persistence or cryptographic consumers that expect primitive strings.
rootCause: Encoding validation accepts coercible values and persists them without a primitive-string type check.

fix.explanation: Require primitive strings before applying canonical regex validation to the DKG session hash, transcript hash, and candidate group key, preventing regex coercion and persistence of non-string values.

title: Unbounded Abort Reason Amplifies State

sourceLocations.note: The abort path writes the unchecked reason directly into the failure record.

triageResult.reasoning:
The finding correctly observes that the abort handlers store event.reason verbatim, but the reason field is purely diagnostic and never drives a security-critical decision. The reducers' abort logic only checks the event type/phase and optional blamedIdx; the actual phase transition, terminal state, and liveness outcome are independent of the reason content. A whole-repo search for failure.reason readers returns only the three write sites (courtDkgMachine.ts:167-176, courtVoteMachine.ts:286-290, courtSigningMachine.ts:252-261) plus test/PoC prints, so no in-scope code consumes the reason for authorization, value transfer, or liveness. The attacker must supply every byte that ends up in state, and abort is terminal so the payload cannot be duplicated inside the machine. That makes the surviving impact bounded, fund-loss-free, and below the security materiality bar.
Evidence: Sink sites: courtDkgMachine.ts:167-176 copies event.reason into failure without runtime validation; courtVoteMachine.ts:286-290 and courtSigningMachine.ts:252-261 do the same. No in-scope consumer: grep for failure.reason across the repository returns only those three write sites and the draft's own PoC files (poc_reason.ts, poc_reason2.ts); no production code reads state.failure.reason for a security decision. Other variable-length inputs are bounded at create/finalize (e.g., courtDkgMachine.ts:135-149, 221-223), but the reason is never similarly guarded.

description: Abort reasons are copied directly into persistent reducer state with no runtime type or size validation. The event type only declares `reason: string`; a caller can supply an arbitrarily large string or a non-string object at runtime, and the reducer stores it in `failure` before returning the new state. Because abort is a terminal transition for valid failure phases, this payload can be retained by storage and propagated through logs or replication as part of the terminal record. The machine has no bound comparable to the bounded identifiers and outcomes enforced elsewhere in the library.
impact: A host-facing attacker can use a single abort to amplify memory, persistence, replication, or logging costs with an oversized reason, potentially causing resource exhaustion. Non-string reasons can also break serializers or downstream code that assumes failure reasons are canonical text.
rootCause: Abort metadata is trusted from the erased TypeScript type and written into state without runtime validation or a bounded representation.

title: Malformed Events Bypass Controlled Rejection

sourceLocations.note: The reducer dereferences the runtime event before validating its shape or discriminant.
Unsupported non-null events fall through rather than being rejected.

triageResult.reasoning:
The reducer does dereference event.type without a runtime shape guard at courtDkgMachine.ts:166, and our runtime test confirms that null/undefined throw a native TypeError while non-string/unknown types silently return the input state. However, the availability impact is bounded by the surrounding architecture: the README and courtInbox.ts classify the public inbound event boundary as a total, non-throwing validator (classifyInboundEvent at courtInbox.ts:394-462), and the library is documented as a pure I/O-free reducer that receives host-injected, already-validated events. No in-scope production path feeds untrusted relay events directly into reduceCourtDkgMachine without validation. The deviated contract is a defensive-coding gap, not an exploitable liveness failure, because any malformed input reaches the reducer only if the host has already bypassed the intended boundary. The silent fall-through for unknown types is equally a no-op, not a state transition. I therefore classify it as a code-quality issue below the security materiality bar.
Evidence: courtDkgMachine.ts:162-275 (no runtime shape guard; null/undefined throw TypeError, unknown types fall through to return state); README.md:158-162 (reducers are pure, host-injected, carry no I/O); courtInbox.ts:394-462 (classifyInboundEvent is total over unknown shape and returns a typed rejection reason without throwing); runtime tests show the only crash is null/undefined, and all other malformed inputs return the original state unchanged.

description: The reducer assumes that every runtime event is a non-null object, despite receiving host-supplied values at a persistence and transport boundary. A `null` event, primitive, or object without a usable `type` reaches `event.type` before any validation and can throw a native `TypeError`; an unknown object instead falls through silently. The public API promises a typed transition error for invalid transitions, but malformed runtime input bypasses that error contract. If a host processes untrusted queue or relay deliveries in the reducer's call path without wrapping native exceptions, one malformed delivery can terminate the dispatch worker or prevent subsequent DKG events from being processed.
impact: Malformed input can cause availability failure in a host that treats reducer exceptions as fatal, while the related unknown-type path silently drops messages. This can stall the ceremony and lead to deadline expiry rather than a controlled abort or retry.
rootCause: There is no runtime event-shape guard before discriminant dispatch, and malformed input is not normalized to `CourtDkgTransitionError`.

title: Default DKG Exposes Every Secret Share

sourceLocations.note: The adapter creates all participant state, computes all final shares, and returns them.
All juror coefficients and commitments are generated in the same process.
The default exported keygen entrypoint instantiates the local adapter.

triageResult.reasoning: The client’s “Single-process ceremony (prototype)” statement explicitly acknowledges that demo coordinators observe every share and that compromise exposes them. The repository also makes cross-client execution on independent juror devices a production gate and requires production consumers to run the ceremony distributed.

description: `PedersenDkgAdapter.run` constructs every participant's private polynomial in `createParticipants`, computes every participant's final share, and returns the complete `shares` array to its caller. `generateFrostKeys` unconditionally instantiates this adapter, so the package's default key-generation entrypoint is a single-process trusted dealer rather than a distributed DKG. The comments acknowledge that production should run independent instances, but no type, runtime guard, or separate production-safe default prevents an integrator from using this entrypoint for live attestations. Any compromise of that process or any caller holding the returned result exposes enough shares to reconstruct the threshold signing capability.
impact: A compromised coordinator, application server, or persistence layer holding the result can obtain the complete set of FROST shares and produce valid attestations for arbitrary Court messages. Downstream systems that treat the group signature as authorization can therefore accept forged verdicts until the group key is rotated.
rootCause: The default key-generation API exposes a centralized implementation and all secret shares through `PedersenDkgAdapter.run()` instead of enforcing a distributed per-juror custody boundary.

title: Noncontiguous Rosters Produce Unusable Records

sourceLocations.note: No sequential-index validation is performed.
The caller's arbitrary indices are preserved in all returned share and record structures.
Canonical recovery rejects verification/VSS indices that are not exactly 1..n.

triageResult.reasoning:
The adapter's validateParams does not enforce the 1..n sequential format that courtRecovery requires, but the only producer of noncontiguous indices is the caller/host. The downstream reader at courtRecovery.ts:758-769 is a fail-closed guard that throws `dkg_record_malformed` and moves no value; it does not authorize any cross-principal transfer, liveness decision, or state change for another party. The entire impact is therefore self-inflicted resource consumption and a recoverable API error, below the security materiality bar. The correct classification is a code-quality/API-contract inconsistency, not a vulnerability.
Evidence: dkg.ts:441-455 accepts arbitrary positive juror indices without contiguity check; courtRecovery.ts:758-769 rejects non-1..n indices with a `dkg_record_malformed` throw; no downstream reader consumes the malformed indices for any cross-principal authorization or value transfer.

description: The adapter accepts arbitrary positive index sets even though the surrounding Court record format requires sequential one-based indices. `validateParams` checks neither contiguity nor an upper bound, and `run` preserves the supplied indices in shares, verification shares, and VSS commitments. A valid call such as indices `[1, 3, 4]` therefore returns a record whose arrays contain those noncontiguous indices. The repository's DKG recovery certification explicitly rejects any verification or VSS index that is not exactly `offset + 1`, so adapter output can be generated successfully and then fail when restored or certified.
impact: An attacker or malformed host input can consume key-generation resources and obtain apparently valid material that cannot pass the package's recovery/certification path. This creates a reproducible ceremony DoS and makes the adapter's output format inconsistent with the canonical Court roster format.
rootCause: The adapter and the canonical record consumer enforce different participant-index invariants.

title: Mutable State Bypasses Frozen Vote Configuration

sourceLocations.note: The returned configuration and ledgers are mutable runtime arrays despite readonly TypeScript types.
Commit/reveal roster admission trusts the exposed participant array.
Reveal admission trusts the exposed allowlist array.
Tally consumes the exposed reveal ledger without revalidation.

triageResult.reasoning: `createCourtVoteMachine` shallow-copies `participantIndices` and `allowedOutcomes` with `[...]` and returns them directly in the state object (courtVoteMachine.ts:214-260). TypeScript `readonly` is erased at runtime, so a holder of the state reference can mutate `state.participantIndices` to admit an unauthorized voter, mutate `state.allowedOutcomes` to allow a previously disallowed outcome, or mutate `state.reveals` to fabricate/alter supporting evidence before `finalize_tally`. The reducer reads these arrays directly at courtVoteMachine.ts:188-191 (roster), courtVoteMachine.ts:345-347 (allowlist), and courtVoteMachine.ts:405-435 (tally), without revalidation or a frozen snapshot. The resulting `verdictHash` is consumed by the signing machine (courtSigningMachine.ts:64, 133-141), so mutable state can cross a host boundary and alter the authorized tally.

description: The constructor copies the input arrays, but it does not freeze the arrays stored in the returned state, and every reducer transition later trusts those arrays directly. A holder of the state reference can therefore append an unauthorized participant index or outcome after creation, or edit the commit/reveal ledgers, without passing any reducer validation. For example, mutating `state.allowedOutcomes` before reveal admission makes a previously disallowed outcome pass `includes`; mutating `state.participantIndices` similarly changes the certified roster used by both commit and reveal admission. The module documentation calls the outcome set frozen, but the returned object provides no runtime immutability enforcement.
impact: If state crosses an untrusted persistence, plugin, worker, or integration boundary, the boundary can rewrite the roster or allowlist after ceremony creation and cause an unauthorized outcome to be admitted and tallied. Ledger mutation can also fabricate or alter supporting reveals before tally finalization, changing the verdict without a valid commit/reveal transition.
rootCause: The constructor performs shallow array copies but does not apply runtime freezing or otherwise encapsulate state, while later transitions trust the exposed mutable arrays. TypeScript `readonly` annotations do not enforce immutability at runtime.

fix.explanation: Freeze the complete vote-machine state graph at creation and after every reducer transition, including configuration arrays, commit/reveal records and ledgers, verdict support IDs, and failure/verdict objects. This preserves reducer behavior while preventing holders of returned state references from mutating the frozen configuration or fabricating ledger contents.

title: Reveal deadline can be bypassed with non-monotonic timestamps

sourceLocations.note: Expiration is only triggered by a separately dispatched tick.
Opening reveals has no `revealDeadline` comparison.
Reveal admission validates only the current event's timestamp.
A late-open phase can be closed; an empty closed ledger cannot finalize.
`assertNow` validates only timestamp shape and `assertBeforeDeadline` compares only the current event timestamp.
`close_commits` permits closure at any time at or after the commit deadline, and `open_reveals` performs no reveal-deadline comparison.
Reveal admission trusts the individual event's pre-deadline `now` and appends the valid reveal to the ledger.
A current-time close freezes the ledger, and finalization tallies all accepted reveals; `reveal_closed` is not expired by tick.
`tick` expires `reveal_open` only when its own event timestamp reaches the deadline, while terminal-state handling occurs after the timestamp-independent abort path.

triageResult.reasoning: Confirmed by judge and critic: open_reveals has no revealDeadline check, so a host can transition to reveal_open after the real deadline. Each accept_reveal only checks its own event.now, and the reducer tracks no max observed time, so a stale pre-deadline reveal can be admitted after the window has closed. The late reveal then flows into close_reveals and finalize_tally. A zero-reveal reveal_closed state is also reachable and cannot be expired by tick. This violates the documented lifecycle deadline guard and is a reducer-level validation flaw, not an acceptable host trust boundary.

description: The state machine allows `open_reveals` from `commit_closed` without checking that `event.now` precedes `revealDeadline`. It also treats timestamps as event-local values: `accept_reveal` checks only the timestamp supplied on that reveal and the state does not retain a maximum observed time. A caller can therefore open the reveal phase after the deadline, submit a cryptographically valid reveal carrying a stale pre-deadline timestamp, then close and finalize the tally using a current timestamp. Because expiration requires a separately dispatched `tick`, event ordering determines whether the machine expires; moreover, a late open and close with no reveals reaches `reveal_closed`, which `tick` intentionally does not expire and which cannot be finalized without a reveal. Enforcing the reveal-window boundary on phase entry and using a monotonic or trusted time source for all deadline-sensitive transitions resolves both the late-admission and stuck-state paths.
impact: An actor able to control reducer event ordering and timestamps can include reveals after the reveal window has actually elapsed, changing the records used to derive the verdict. The same deadline bypass can also leave a ceremony permanently in `reveal_closed` with no valid reveal, preventing tally finalization.
rootCause: `open_reveals` lacks a `revealDeadline` guard, while deadline checks trust independent caller-supplied `event.now` values rather than enforcing monotonic or trusted time across transitions.

fix.explanation: Track the greatest timestamp observed by the vote reducer, reject timestamp rollback on every time-bearing event, and require reveal-phase entry before the reveal deadline. This closes both stale-time reveal admission and late-open empty-ledger paths.

triageResult.reasoning: Confirmed by judge and critic: finalize_tally uses JavaScript's UTF-16 string comparison (`outcome < winner`) for tie-breaking, while outcomes are canonicalized as UTF-8 by CanonicalWriter.text before hashing. description: Allowed outcomes may contain arbitrary bounded Unicode text, while equal-count outcomes are selected with JavaScript's `<` operator. These orderings differ for valid values such as `U+10000` and `U+E000`: a JavaScript reducer can select `U+10000`, whereas a client comparing UTF-8 bytes or Unicode scalar values can select `U+E000`. The selected outcome is incorporated into `verdictHash`, so this is a consensus-relevant result difference rather than a display discrepancy. impact: Independent implementations can derive different winners and verdict hashes from the same tied reveal ledger. Their attestations, verification, signing, settlement, or other downstream decision processing can then reject one another's result or act on conflicting court outcomes.
rootCause: Tie resolution uses JavaScript's UTF-16 string comparator without an explicitly specified canonical ordering consistent with the UTF-8 representation used by the protocol.

fix.explanation: Defines the protocol tie-break as lexicographic unsigned UTF-8 byte order and applies that comparator when tied reveal counts are resolved, aligning winner selection with canonical outcome serialization.

The `abort` branch at `courtVoteMachine.ts:286-290` does copy `event.reason` into `state.failure.reason` without runtime validation, so the claimed mechanism is technically accurate. However, the only security-relevant state change in that branch is `phase: 'aborted'`; the `reason` value is never used in a guard, canonical hash, tally, or downstream authorization/liveness decision. The documented integration model has hosts persist returned reducer states, so a circular reason can make JSON serialization fail and malformed or oversized values can cross into storage, logging, or failure handling. Validate that the reason is a primitive bounded string at the transition boundary and reject or normalize invalid input before constructing `failure`.
impact: A caller able to provide abort events can cause hosts that serialize the returned state to fail on circular values, interrupting durable recording of the aborted terminal state. The reducer is explicitly a pure, I/O-free state machine with no network access and no source-event timestamp field (courtVoteMachine.ts:12-14). The tally and verdict only consume the outcome and reveal event IDs, not any source-event chronology (courtVoteMachine.ts:408-435). The actual privacy violation—publicly disclosing a reveal before the commit phase—is a network-level act by the participant that the reducer cannot observe or prevent, and the reducer's acceptance of a well-formed reveal during the reveal phase is the intended behavior. Because the temporal-ordering violation has no material reader in the reducer, the impact is theoretical.

impact: A participant can disclose a vote and salt before making the corresponding commitment while still having that vote accepted after a matching commitment is inserted. rootCause: The reducer does not store or compare authenticated commit and reveal event chronology, so `accept_reveal` enforces processing order and hash equality rather than the required publication-time ordering.

title: Use rejection sampling for unbiased deterministic scalars

sourceLocations.note: The HKDF output is reduced modulo the scalar order and only zero residues are retried.
`modN` implements direct remainder reduction.
The seeded derivation reduces each 512-bit HKDF result and rejects only zero.

triageResult.reasoning: Although direct reduction is not perfectly uniform, reducing a 512-bit sample modulo a roughly 256-bit order has statistical distance below approximately 2^-258 per sample. Exploiting or even distinguishing that bias requires an infeasible number of samples and provides no realistic material impact.

description: `seededScalar` maps each 512-bit HKDF output through `modN` and retries only when the resulting residue is `0`. Because `2^512` is not an exact multiple of the secp256k1 scalar order, direct modular reduction gives some nonzero scalar values one more preimage than others. The `uint16` counter prevents counter truncation or rollover collisions, but it does not make the sampling distribution uniform. This contradicts the helper documentation's claim that the counter-based derivation avoids modulo bias. Replace the residue-based retry with rejection sampling of the unreduced HKDF integer against an order-aligned range, then derive the nonzero scalar from an accepted sample.
impact: Consumers relying on `seededScalar` as a uniform deterministic scalar sampler receive a small, systematic statistical bias in derived coefficients or keys. The reviewed helper is documented for deterministic demo, test, or secret-seed use, but its public uniformity guarantee is not met for direct or future callers.
rootCause: `seededScalar` reduces fixed-width HKDF output modulo `SCALAR_ORDER` and rejects only `0` rather than rejecting values outside an exact order-aligned sampling range.

description: `verifyProofOfKnowledge` accepts `proof.response` as an arbitrary-length integer and only checks the resulting algebraic equality. rootCause: `verifyProofOfKnowledge` omits fixed-length canonical encoding and group-order range validation for `proof.response` before scalar multiplication.

description: `wrapProtocolEventWithSigner` encrypts the caller-selected rumor into `sealContent`, but accepts any valid kind-`13` seal returned by the external signer because it never compares `sealCandidate.content` with that ciphertext. A malicious signer can therefore return a valid seal for different content, or use getters, proxies, or serialization behavior to make the wrapped bytes differ from those that were checked. impact: A compromised or malicious external signer can cause recipients to receive a stale or attacker-selected internally valid protocol rumor instead of the event the host submitted for wrapping. rootCause: The function neither requires the verified `sealCandidate.content` to equal the requested `sealContent` nor reuses the verified plain candidate when serializing the gift wrap.

fix.explanation: Bind the external signer's verified seal to the exact requested ciphertext, deep-copy its tags into the reconstructed plain event, and pass only that verified candidate to NIP-59 wrapping so signer-controlled serialization cannot alter the checked seal.

title: Unbounded gift-wrap batches exhaust signer processing

sourceLocations.note: The unbounded batch is processed sequentially and deduplicated only after each unwrap.
Each addressed item can invoke public-key retrieval and two external NIP-44 decryptions.
Unbounded input array is iterated and each item is unwrapped.
Deduplication and filtering occur only after decryption work.

triageResult.reasoning:
The finding correctly describes that `unwrapProtocolEventsWithSigner` iterates the entire caller-supplied `wraps` array and performs expensive per-item cryptographic work before deduplication/filtering. However, the scoped component is a pure library helper with no network boundary, no persistence, and no signer queue of its own. The README explicitly states the package contains no networking beyond event builders/parsers and that hosts inject transport and storage (`README.md:11-13`). The `wraps` array is therefore supplied by the host caller, and the function merely returns a filtered, deduplicated projection to that caller (`courtSigner.ts:245-258`) without holding any committed state or making a cross-principal liveness/authorization decision. The entire surviving impact is bounded by whatever array the host chooses to pass, is recoverable by the host limiting batch sizes, and does not corrupt committed state or bypass any authorization gate. It is a missing application-level resource limit rather than a material library-level security defect.
Evidence: README.md:11-13 (library has no networking; hosts inject transport/storage); courtSigner.ts:245-258 (function returns a pure filtered/deduplicated projection to the caller, with no persistent state or cross-principal decision)

description: `unwrapProtocolEventsWithSigner` accepts a caller-supplied `wraps` array without imposing a maximum count or aggregate work budget. It processes every element sequentially by invoking `unwrapProtocolEventWithSigner` before checking the resulting rumor ID against `seen`. For addressed gift wraps, that helper calls `signer.getPublicKey()` and can perform two `signer.nip44Decrypt` operations, along with parsing and verification work. Consequently, malformed inputs still incur per-item dispatch work, while repeated valid wraps are fully decrypted before post-decryption deduplication suppresses their output. A batch-size or work-budget limit, with duplicate-wrap rejection where safely available before signer operations, is needed to bound this processing path.
impact: An attacker able to influence batch input can submit arbitrarily large arrays, including repeated valid wraps, to drive unbounded signer/RPC requests and cryptographic processing. This can monopolize the signer queue and delay legitimate Court private-message processing.
rootCause: The batch API has no input-count or work-budget limit, and its `seen` deduplication occurs only after the expensive per-item unwrap operation.

Construction therefore succeeds for malformed raw key material, while public-key derivation, signing, or NIP-44 ECDH subsequently causes the cryptographic dependency to reject it. Validating scalar range at each raw-secret entry point, preferably through a shared validation routine, would reject invalid material at the custody boundary.
impact: A host that accepts corrupted or attacker-controlled raw key material can retain an apparently initialized but unusable signer. Later public-key derivation, event signing, or NIP-44 encryption and decryption can fail at an operation-dependent point, disrupting setup or availability without producing an unauthorized valid key.
rootCause: Raw-secret constructors enforce only a 32-byte length and omit validation that the secp256k1 scalar satisfies `1 <= d < n`.

The draft's core claim is accurate: `unwrapProtocolEventWithSigner` at courtSigner.ts:212-223 returns a rumor after only record-shape, seal-author, string-id, and `getEventHash` equality checks; it never validates that `kind` or `created_at` are canonical, safe, integral numbers. `getEventHash` (nostr-tools/lib/esm/pure.js:92-95) serializes via `JSON.stringify`, which accepts non-integer finite numbers (e.g. `1.5`, `1e20`) and preserves them through the wire, so the returned `NostrEvent` can carry noncanonical finite numeric fields. However, the draft's impact is bounded below the materiality bar: the only in-repo consumers are `unwrapProtocolEventsWithSigner` (kind/dispute filter + id dedup) at courtSigner.ts:246-257 and `CourtInbox.drain` (id merge + `created_at` sort) at courtInbox.ts:683-725. Neither moves value, authorizes a cross-principal operation, or gates a consequential/liveness commit. The `getEventHash` check canonicalizes values before hashing, so any same-id collision is over duplicate canonical content; a malicious sender cannot create two semantically distinct messages with the same id. The host is documented as the boundary that authenticates and dispatches events, and any downstream state machine already receives the raw returned event. The absence of an in-scope reader that consumes these noncanonical numbers for a value transfer, authorization, or recovery decision makes the surviving effect sub-material.

description: The rumor unwrap path treats `getEventHash` as both an integrity check and validation of the event's numeric fields. It verifies the seal author, requires an `id` string, and compares the computed hash, but does not require `kind` and `created_at` to be finite, safe, integral, canonical values. The underlying serializer accepts JavaScript numbers and uses `JSON.stringify`, which converts non-finite values such as `1e400` (parsed as `Infinity`) to `null` and normalizes `-0` to `0`. An authorized sender can compute an ID over this normalized serialization, encrypt and sign the rumor, and cause unwrap to return a rumor whose received JSON representation is noncanonical. Consequently, distinct wire representations can be accepted with the same ID even though the ID is expected to commit to the rumor's exact contents.
impact: An authorized sender can inject rumors with malformed `kind` or `created_at` fields and produce representation collisions in ID-based batch or inbox deduplication. Consumers that order rumors by `created_at` or assume returned `NostrEvent` numeric fields are conventional finite integers may misprocess malformed data or discard one of the colliding messages.
rootCause: `getEventHash` is relied on as a schema-validation gate even though its serializer accepts noncanonical JavaScript numeric values and normalizes them during serialization.

title: Raw signer secrets cannot be deterministically cleared

sourceLocations.note: The signer retains a copied secret and initializes the NIP-44 helper.
The helper independently copies and retains the secret.

triageResult.reasoning:
The draft correctly notes that SeckeyCourtSigner and Nip44SeckeyCrypto each retain independent copies of a 32-byte raw secret and expose no deterministic zeroization or disposal lifecycle. However, the code itself scopes this adapter to non-production contexts: SeckeyCourtSigner is explicitly "Provided for tests, demo rooms, and local tooling — production jurors should use a real external signer" (courtSigner.ts:92-96). The production boundary is CourtEventSigner, whose interface contract is that implementations "MUST NOT expose the secret key" (courtSigner.ts:56-57), and the README lists the file as "external-signer transport (NIP-07/NIP-46): no raw nsec" (README.md:292). Because the entire path the finding describes begins only in the local/test adapter, and the intended production custody path never holds the raw secret in this process, the surviving impact is bounded to demo/test/local tooling. There is no production fund-custody path, no cross-principal authorization decision, and no liveness path that depends on this retained secret. The missing lifecycle is therefore a hardening gap in a deliberately non-production helper, not a material vulnerability in the scoped private-transport component.
Evidence: courtSigner.ts:92-96 (class scoped to tests, demos, and local tooling); courtSigner.ts:56-57 (CourtEventSigner production contract forbids secret exposure); courtSigner.ts:97-110 and nip44Crypto.ts:18-35 (two retained copies); README.md:292 (transport is external-signer, no raw nsec)

description: `SeckeyCourtSigner` copies the supplied raw secret into `this.seckey` and constructs `Nip44SeckeyCrypto` from that value. `Nip44SeckeyCrypto` independently normalizes and retains another `Uint8Array` containing the same secret. Neither class provides a disposal or zeroization lifecycle through which callers can clear these buffers after a demo, test, or local-tool session. Garbage collection cannot provide deterministic erasure, leaving both copies resident for an indeterminate period. A disposal operation should clear each owned buffer and prevent subsequent use, with the signer delegating cleanup to its helper.
impact: A memory disclosure or compromise of a long-lived process may recover the raw secret after the caller is done with the signer. Retaining two independently owned copies increases the period and number of locations from which key material can remain recoverable.
rootCause: `SeckeyCourtSigner` and `Nip44SeckeyCrypto` retain independent raw-secret buffers without an explicit zeroization or disposal lifecycle.

title: Out-of-range attempt values crash signing initialization

sourceLocations.note: The constructor accepts any non-negative safe-integer attempt and immediately hashes it.
The canonical encoder used by the hash rejects values above the u32 maximum.

triageResult.reasoning: createCourtSigningMachine validates attempt as any non-negative safe integer (courtSigningMachine.ts:211-213) but then calls hashCourtSigningSession, which encodes attempt via CanonicalWriter.u32 (courtSigningMachine.ts:148). CanonicalWriter.u32 rejects values above 0xffffffff with CourtSessionValidationError (courtSession.ts:402-411). The throw happens before any CourtSigningMachineState is returned (courtSigningMachine.ts:217-225), so no signing session is created, no attestation is produced, and no security or liveness decision is affected. The entire impact is a single unexpected exception type in one host call.

description: `createCourtSigningMachine` accepts every non-negative safe integer for `attempt`, including values greater than `4294967295`. It immediately supplies the accepted value to `hashCourtSigningSession`, whose canonical encoding uses `CanonicalWriter.u32`. That encoder rejects integers above `0xffffffff`, so values accepted by the constructor throw a lower-level `CourtSessionValidationError` rather than producing the initial state or a `CourtSigningTransitionError`. The public validation domain for `attempt` therefore disagrees with the domain required to construct the canonical signing-session identity. Enforcing the `u32` range at the constructor boundary, or consistently adopting a wider encoding, resolves the mismatch.
impact: A host that forwards an attacker-controlled or persisted out-of-range `attempt` can reliably fail signing-attempt initialization after the constructor has explicitly accepted the value. Repeated malformed creation requests can disrupt signing setup for the affected dispute and may route execution through an uncaught-error path rather than the expected transition-error handling.
rootCause: `createCourtSigningMachine` validates `attempt` as a non-negative safe integer while `hashCourtSigningSession` encodes it through the narrower `u32` domain.

title: Malformed nonce commitments can poison FROST signing

sourceLocations.note: The point predicate is a syntax-only regular expression.
Commitment admission stores regex-matching point strings without point parsing.
The authenticated commitment-event parser applies the same syntax-only point check.
FROST signing-context construction receives the unparsed commitment collection.
FROST signing-context construction consumes the complete commitment list.
Commitment admission stores regex-matching points without parsing them.
The strict signed-event parser applies the same shape-only point check.
Untrusted public nonce strings are cast into a FROST commitment package.

triageResult.reasoning: The reducer and protocol parser gate nonce commitments only with the syntax-only regex HEX_POINT (courtSigningMachine.ts:114-115, 284-286; courtProtocolEvents.ts:128, 561-572). They do not parse or validate secp256k1 field-range, lift, or curve membership before storing the strings. independentSigning.ts:239-243 casts the untrusted strings into a frost.CommitmentPackage, and signing.ts:200-204 feeds them to frost.Lib.get_group_signing_ctx. A runtime test confirmed that the reducer accepts a syntactically valid compressed point not on the curve and the FROST library throws 'bad point: is not on curve, sqrt error'. A malicious roster participant can therefore poison a signing attempt and prevent honest coordinators from producing an attestation.

description: Nonce commitments are validated with `HEX_POINT`, which checks only lowercase hexadecimal shape, length, and an optional `02` or `03` prefix rather than whether the value represents a secp256k1 point. The signed-event parser and the signing-state reducer both rely on this predicate, so an authenticated roster participant can submit a syntactically valid commitment whose coordinate is out of range or cannot be lifted to the curve. Those strings are retained in commitment records, and the independent signing path also casts them directly to `frost.CommitmentPackage`. The resulting commitment collection is passed to `get_group_signing_ctx`, where downstream FROST point processing must consume the malformed values. Validation must parse the permitted x-only or compressed representations and reject values that fail field-range, lift, and curve-membership checks before they are admitted or frozen.
impact: A selected roster participant can publish a correctly signed malformed nonce commitment and poison a signing attempt containing that commitment. FROST context creation, reveal, partial signing, or aggregation can then reject or throw, requiring the coordinator to abort or restart the attempt. Repeating this behavior can prevent dispute attestations from being produced while the participant remains unable to forge a valid signature.
rootCause: `HEX_POINT` is used as proof of a valid secp256k1 nonce point even though neither the protocol boundary nor commitment admission performs cryptographic point validation.

fix.explanation: Adds shared cryptographic validation for canonical x-only or compressed secp256k1 points and applies it before nonce commitments enter signed-event parsing, reducer state, independent signing state, or restored snapshots.

title: Duplicate persisted records bypass distinct-signer thresholds

sourceLocations.note: Persisted state contains raw commitment records and the later frozen signer set.

triageResult.reasoning: The reducer's threshold-sensitive transitions rely on raw array length rather than distinct roster-valid indices. `close_commitments` (`courtSigningMachine.ts:311-323`) checks `state.commitments.length < state.threshold` and maps every record to `finalizedSignerSet` without uniqueness or roster validation, so duplicate commitments (e.g., two records for idx 1) can satisfy a threshold of 2 and produce a non-distinct signer set such as `[1,1]`. `aggregate` (`courtSigningMachine.ts:358-371`) checks `state.partials.length < state.threshold` without distinctness validation, so duplicate partial records can satisfy the threshold with only one distinct signer. description: The reducer trusts restored or directly supplied `CourtSigningMachineState` even though its TypeScript array types do not enforce runtime invariants. impact: An attacker able to influence restored state can make duplicate commitment or partial records satisfy threshold checks and advance the signing flow without the intended number of distinct signers. Duplicate commitments can also finalize a signer set such as `[1, 1]`; because incoming partials are deduplicated by index, the attempt then cannot reach the required partial count and must be restarted. rootCause: `reduceCourtSigningMachine` relies on array lengths in `close_commitments` and `aggregate` without runtime validation that persisted commitment and partial records represent distinct, valid, mutually consistent participants.

fix.explanation: Adds a single reducer-entry invariant boundary that rejects invalid or duplicate commitment/partial records and requires any finalized signer set to exactly match the distinct sorted commitment indices, preventing raw array lengths from satisfying thresholds with duplicate restored records.

sourceLocations.snippet:
Three pure, fail-closed reducers model the ceremony. Each is
`create*Machine(params)` + `reduce*Machine(state, event)` with an injected
clock, a typed `*TransitionError`, terminal-phase rejection, and explicit
`tick`/`abort` events. They carry no I/O — hosts feed them events and

triageResult.reasoning: `createCourtSigningMachine` validates `deadline` as a positive safe integer at `courtSigningMachine.ts:214-216`, but `reduceCourtSigningMachine` accepts caller-supplied or restored `CourtSigningMachineState` and immediately uses `state.deadline` in `assertBeforeDeadline` without re-validating it. `assertBeforeDeadline` (`courtSigningMachine.ts:169-174`) only validates `now` and then compares `now >= state.deadline`. JavaScript relational comparisons against `NaN`, `Infinity`, or `undefined` evaluate to `false`, so a malformed deadline bypasses every timestamped transition including `start`, `accept_commitment`, `close_commitments`, `accept_partial`, `aggregate`, and `publish`. This defeats the ceremony's time-bound liveness/state-integrity invariant, allowing a state with a malformed deadline to reach `attestation_published` even with late `now` values. The Trust Model Map explicitly states the host is not trusted to alter reducer state transitions outside the reducer's validation, so the missing re-validation is a reducer bug.

description: `createCourtSigningMachine` requires a positive safe-integer `deadline`, but `reduceCourtSigningMachine` accepts its `state` argument without runtime validation. `assertBeforeDeadline` validates only `now` and uses `now >= state.deadline`; with an omitted deadline, `NaN`, or `Infinity`, this comparison can evaluate false rather than reject the state. Consequently, a malformed state restored or otherwise supplied by a host can pass `start` and each later timestamped transition, including `aggregate` and `publish`, after the intended deadline. The separate `tick` path does not establish the invariant for normal transitions because it is optional and also relies on a direct comparison with the unvalidated value. Validate the persisted state's deadline before processing every reducer event, or make `assertBeforeDeadline` reject values that are not positive safe integers before comparing them.
impact: A host that restores corrupted or attacker-modified state can progress an expired signing attempt through aggregation and publish an attestation without an enforceable time bound. This defeats the ceremony's deadline invariant for consumers that treat reducer transitions as authoritative, causing an integrity and liveness failure rather than a direct custody loss in the scoped library.
rootCause: `reduceCourtSigningMachine` trusts runtime `state.deadline` values that were not created by `createCourtSigningMachine`, while `assertBeforeDeadline` compares them using JavaScript relational semantics without validating them.

fix.explanation: Adds a shared positive-safe-integer deadline assertion and invokes it at the reducer boundary before every event, so malformed persisted deadlines fail closed across tick, abort, terminal, and normal transitions while preserving valid-state behavior.

If an honest juror produces a commitment for session A, the same proof is only useful in session B if the exact same commitment/nonce pair is also accepted for session B. triageResult.reasoning:
The finding correctly observes that `verifyFinalSignature` at crypto.ts:144-155 can throw on malformed `groupPubkey`, `messageHex`, or `signatureHex`, while `verifySchnorr` at crypto.ts:157-170 catches equivalent parse failures and returns `false`. However, within the requested implementation scope, this behavior is sub-material. First, a completed whole-repo reader search shows the helper is never called by any production path in the scoped code; it is only exercised by test files (`__tests__/dkg.test.ts`, `__tests__/independentDkg.test.ts`, `__tests__/independentSigning.test.ts`, `__tests__/signing.test.ts`) and exported as a public utility at `index.ts:36`. The actual production signing verification path uses the underlying `frost.Lib.verify_final_sig` directly at `signing.ts:300-304` with internally-produced inputs (the group key from the DKG record, the message, and the aggregated signature), so the helper's exception semantics do not gate any in-scope liveness, authorization, or value-transfer decision. Second, the same unwrapped FROST context pattern appears in `aggregatePublicNonce` at `crypto.ts:131-142`, which also calls `frost.Lib.get_group_key_context(groupPubkey)` without a try/catch, so the module does not uniformly catch FROST parse exceptions; the inconsistency with `verifySchnorr` is therefore not evidence of a missing universal contract. The finding's impact—crashing a request, worker, or batch—depends on an external caller invoking this specific helper with unvalidated input and no surrounding exception boundary, which is not realized anywhere in the requested scope.
Evidence: crypto.ts:144-155 (verifyFinalSignature throws on malformed inputs), crypto.ts:131-142 (aggregatePublicNonce uses the same unwrapped frost.Lib.get_group_key_context pattern), signing.ts:300-304 (production signing verification uses frost.Lib.verify_final_sig directly, not the helper), index.ts:36 (helper is exported but no in-scope production caller exists), whole-repo grep confirms only test callers and the export consume verifyFinalSignature

description: The exported `verifyFinalSignature(groupPubkey, messageHex, signatureHex)` helper in `crypto.ts` is documented as a boolean verifier, but it calls `frost.Lib.get_group_key_context(groupPubkey)` and `hexToBytes(...)` on user-supplied strings without any exception boundary. Invalid public-key encodings can throw during FROST context construction, and malformed hex can throw before the dependency's verifier runs. The adjacent `verifySchnorr()` helper explicitly catches parse failures and returns `false`, demonstrating inconsistent malformed-input failure semantics across the public verification API. As a result, callers who rely on the boolean contract must add their own catch blocks to prevent a malformed attestation from aborting a request, worker, or batch.
impact: Malformed relay or API attestation inputs can escape the predicate as an exception rather than a clean rejection. In integrations that treat the helper as a pure boolean verifier, a single malformed signature can terminate a request, worker, or batch instead of being rejected as invalid, producing a verification-path availability failure under repeated malicious input.
rootCause: `verifyFinalSignature()` delegates parsing and FROST verification of untrusted inputs without wrapping the call path in a try/catch that maps parse/dependency failures to its declared `false` return value.

const HEX_32 = /^[0-9a-f]{64}$/;

triageResult.reasoning:
The draft correctly identifies that RegExp.prototype.test coerces its argument to a string, so a String object or a one-element array whose toString yields 64 hex characters passes the reducer's HEX_32 check. However, the terminal actor reaching the commit/reveal sink is the authenticated roster participant, not an arbitrary external principal. The reducer explicitly delegates Nostr author authentication and author-to-roster mapping to the host boundary (courtVoteMachine.ts:12-14), and the only in-reducer gate on `accept_commit` is `assertParticipant(state, event.idx)` (courtVoteMachine.ts:188-191, invoked at courtVoteMachine.ts:296-299). That means the only way to append a malformed commit for a given index is for the authenticated participant for that index (or a host already mis-mapping authors) to supply it. The strict-equality mismatch at courtVoteMachine.ts:362 therefore blocks the same participant's own reveal—self-grief, with no committed cross-principal state and no denial of another principal's legitimate path. The sessionHash path is supplied by the host at `createCourtVoteMachine` (courtVoteMachine.ts:201-210); the library's normal session-hash construction already emits a primitive string via `bytesToHex(sha256(...))`, so a non-string sessionHash is a host self-error rather than an attacker-exploitable reducer path. The entire surviving impact is bounded to the acting party's own ceremony or own slot, falling below the materiality bar for a cross-principal security issue.

description: The `courtVoteMachine` reducer uses `HEX_32.test(...)` to validate `sessionHash`, `commitHash`, `eventId`, and `salt` fields, but `RegExp.prototype.test` coerces its argument to a string. As a result, a boxed `String`, a one-element string array, or any other object whose `toString()` yields 64 lowercase hex characters passes validation and is stored verbatim in `CourtVoteMachineState`. The commit comparison `existing.commitHash === event.commitHash` and the reveal comparison `expected !== commit.commitHash` both use strict equality, so a stored non-string commit can never match the primitive string produced by `hashCourtVoteCommit`. A malformed event therefore consumes the participant's single allowed commit slot and permanently blocks that index's reveal, or it introduces a non-string `eventId`/`salt` that later breaks canonical encoding and serialization. The same defect applies to `sessionHash` at creation, deferring failure until a valid reveal is processed. TypeScript `string` annotations are erased at runtime, so the reducer must perform explicit `typeof value === 'string'` checks before the regex or store canonicalized strings.
impact: A host that forwards attacker-shaped parsed values (e.g., arrays or boxed strings) can consume a roster index's one allowed commit slot with an un-revealable record, reducing or preventing valid finalization. It also permits non-string identifiers to reach the reveal ledger and verdict, breaking canonical encoding assumptions and downstream serialization.
rootCause: Hex-format validation uses `RegExp.test` without first asserting `typeof value === 'string'`, and accepted fields are stored without canonicalization or defensive copying.
